match.reason: No point in the bank teaches the matching principle; the closest, financing a new business, covers equity versus debt rather than matching the length of finance to the life of the asset.

draft.title: The matching principle
card: The matching principle says the term of the finance should match how long the business will use the asset. The loan should run for about as long as the asset earns money.
Stock and other current assets are used up or turned into cash within a year. They suit short-term finance, such as an overdraft.
Buildings and heavy machinery last for many years. They suit long-term finance, such as a mortgage or a long lease.

A mismatch causes problems. A long-term asset bought with short-term finance must be repaid before it has earned enough, which can strain cash flow. A short-term need met with long-term finance can leave the business paying interest after the need has ended.
draft.remember: Match the length of the finance to the length of time the asset is used.

a.q: Which choice best follows the matching principle?
opts: Using a mortgage to buy a new factory building
Using an overdraft to buy a new factory building
Using a mortgage to buy extra stock for one sale
Using retained profits to pay for a delivery truck
a.why: A factory building lasts for many years, so long-term finance such as a mortgage suits it. An overdraft is the tempting option because it is quick, but it is short-term and would need repaying long before the building has paid for itself.
a.clue: How long will the asset be used, and how long should the finance last?

b.q: Priya runs a garden shop in Ballarat. She buys extra plants for a six-week spring rush, paying with a 15-year loan. What is the main problem with this choice?
opts: The loan outlasts the need, so interest is paid long after
The loan must be repaid before the plants are sold
The loan gives the lender a share in the shop's ownership
The loan is too quick to arrange for a short-term need
b.why: The plants are a short-term asset, sold within weeks, but the 15-year loan keeps running and costing interest long after. The second option describes the opposite mismatch, where short-term finance funds a long-term asset.
b.clue: Compare how long the plants are held with how long the loan lasts.

a.best: Using a mortgage to buy a new factory building
also_right: Using retained profits to pay for a delivery truck

b.best: The loan outlasts the need, so interest is paid long after

problems.detail: 'Using retained profits to pay for a delivery truck' is defensible as following the matching principle. Retained profits are permanent internal finance, so they suit a long-term asset such as a truck. The option is meant as a distractor but is not clearly wrong. Replace it with a plain mismatch, such as an overdraft for a delivery truck.

Why (b) refers to 'the second option', but the options are shown in random order. Here the second option is the ownership-share distractor, not the opposite-mismatch option ('must be repaid before the plants are sold'). The why should name the option by its content, not its position.
